metadata.title: PISA in Low and Middle Income Countries (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This OECD working paper is primarily a descriptive and policy-oriented synthesis of PISA participation and implementation challenges in low- and middle-income countries, rather than an analysis of student microdata with an explicit estimation pipeline. It discusses PISA’s design features (random sampling of 15-year-olds, contextual questionnaires, and proficiency/probability-based reporting such as Level 2 baselines) but does not specify the use of complex survey weights or replicate-weight variance estimation in an analytic model. Because no student-level modeling/estimation procedure is presented, there is no reported weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) to interpret. For any future empirical replication using PISA microdata, analysts should apply PISA’s complex survey design weights and replicate weights as provided in the international database when estimating population-representative statistics and uncertainty.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The paper does not report an empirical student-level predictive/analytic model that would require explicit plausible-values (PV) handling or a documented missing-data strategy. Instead, it summarizes participation patterns and discusses challenges (e.g., non-representative coverage of 15-year-olds, clustering at low proficiency) and provides illustrative country results (e.g., mean scores and proficiency-level shares) drawn from OECD/PISA reporting. As a result, PV and missing-data handling are not applicable to the paper’s presented evidence base, and the paper does not document a missing-data procedure for an estimation model.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No student-level analytic sample is constructed in this working paper. The paper uses descriptive evidence from OECD documentation, PISA Governing Board materials, semi-structured interviews, and a survey of PGB representatives, and it reports selected PISA 2009 results and trends (e.g., mean reading scores, shares below proficiency Level 2) for illustrative purposes. Therefore, no explicit inclusion/exclusion criteria for an analytic student dataset are provided.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD working paper synthesizes how low- and middle-income partner countries participate in PISA across multiple cycles (with detailed discussion anchored in PISA 2009 and participation patterns up to 2015). It explains that PISA is designed to benchmark 15-year-olds’ reading, mathematics, and science performance using proficiency levels (e.g., Level 2 as a baseline) and contextual questionnaires, but it argues that effective policy use is constrained by implementation and capacity challenges. The paper reports descriptive cross-country patterns: students in many partner countries perform substantially below OECD averages, with large shares below baseline proficiency, and it highlights that coverage of 15-year-olds can be non-universal, reducing representativeness and comparability. It also discusses how national wealth (GNI per capita) relates to performance, noting a flattening relationship at higher income levels. As a non-empirical policy synthesis, it does not estimate ML models, does not report predictive metrics, and does not document PV or missing-data handling for an analytic pipeline.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is a descriptive policy and implementation synthesis rather than an empirical ML study with a defined student-level analytic dataset. Consequently, there is no reported total student sample size, no per-country student counts, no explicit PV/missing-data handling for an estimation model, and no ML algorithms or predictive performance metrics. The paper’s evidence base is drawn from OECD documentation, interviews, and reported PISA results (means and proficiency shares), so the ML-specific fields are intentionally empty.
